issues.legal_issue: A party that knowingly participates without protest in arbitration proceedings despite an agreement-based defect is precluded from challenging the proceedings or award on that ground after an unfavorable award, whereas participation does not bar an objection based on breach of a mandatory legal provision.
material_facts: The parties agreed to the appointment of an arbitrator by official designation to resolve their construction disputes.
After the appointed arbitrator was transferred, he continued the arbitration and made the awards.
The Board knew of the transfer and participated in the proceedings without objecting, including by presenting evidence and having counsel make submissions.

The Board challenged the awards on the ground that the transferred arbitrator lacked authority to continue, but the court found that continuation breached, at most, the parties’ agreement and did not violate a mandatory provision of law.
The High Court allowed the objections and set aside the awards; the Supreme Court reversed that judgment.
issues.conclusion: The Board’s participation without protest precluded its agreement-based challenge to the arbitrator’s continued authority. The High Court was not justified in setting aside the awards, and the appeals were allowed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 30 of the Arbitration Act, 1940, an objection based on a lawful agreement may be raised at the initial stage, and a defect may be corrected then; a party that knows of the defect and nevertheless participates without protest and takes its chances is precluded from challenging the reference, proceedings, or award on that ground after the award. This principle is supported by N. Chellappan v. Secretary, Kerala State Electricity Board, Chowdhri Murtaza Hossin v. Mussumat Bibi Bachunnissa, Prasun Roy v. Calcutta Metropolitan Development Authority, and M/s. Neelakantan & Bros. Construction v. Superintending Engineer, National Highways. There is no estoppel against a mandatory provision of law, as illustrated by State of Punjab v. Hardyal, which concerned the statutory time limit under Section 3 read with Clause 3 of the First Schedule. For a directory legal provision, a party who participates without protest may be precluded from raising the objection after the award.

rule.if: award_challenge_proceeding and lawful_agreement_based_defect and party_knew_defect and party_participated_without_protest and not mandatory_law_breach

predicates.award_challenge_proceeding: A party seeks to challenge the validity of arbitration proceedings or an award.
predicates.lawful_agreement_based_defect: The alleged defect arises from the parties’ lawful agreement governing the arbitration.
predicates.party_knew_defect: The challenging party knew the circumstances giving rise to the alleged defect.
predicates.party_participated_without_protest: The challenging party participated in the arbitration without objecting or reserving its objection.
predicates.mandatory_law_breach: The alleged defect involves a breach of a mandatory legal requirement.

issues.definition: When an award challenge concerns a known defect arising from a lawful agreement, the party participated without protest, and no mandatory legal requirement was breached, the agreement-based objection is precluded.
